archetype.name: Fringe Contender (all offense)
archetype.definition: A top-10 offense with a quarterback who stays clean, attached to one of the league's worst defenses for a second straight year, in a division weak enough that this combination can still contend.

report.headline: Same Cowboys as 2025: elite offense, broken pass defense, and now turnovers creeping in.
report.take:
Dallas is a familiar team. The offense ranks 6th in EPA per play and 5th in success rate, and the defense ranks 31st in EPA allowed and dead last against the pass. That is almost a copy of 2025, when the offense finished 5th and the defense 32nd on the way to seven wins. The 2-4 record isn't a fluke and it isn't a collapse. It is roughly what a team scoring 25.2 and allowing 26.5 a game should look like, with a little bad luck on top. The point differential implies 3.4 wins, and the 25% record in one-score games has cost them about one more.

The offense is built on Dak Prescott throwing from clean pockets. A 2.6% sack rate (2nd) and only 7 sacks taken in six games give him time, and CeeDee Lamb (69 targets) and George Pickens (52) soak up most of the volume. The run game looks worse than it is. Javonte Williams averages 3.33 yards a carry (27th) behind a 26% stuff rate, yet run success is 6th and run EPA 9th, so the ground game keeps the offense on schedule more than the yardage suggests. The real change is ball security. The first four weeks produced 37, 31 and 34-point outings with at most one turnover a game. Tampa Bay and Green Bay then forced five giveaways between them, and pass EPA swung to -3.3 and -8.4.

The numbers hide where the defense actually breaks. It isn't getting beaten deep (16th in deep-pass EPA). It bleeds on short throws (31st) and allows explosive pass plays at the second-worst rate in the league, which points to tackling and coverage after the catch rather than safeties getting burned. Opponents convert 54.7% of third downs, the worst rate in the league. That is why Dallas ranks 30th in time of possession despite an efficient offense. The pass rush (18% pressure, 8 sacks) can't get teams off the field, and only 3 takeaways means it isn't flipping drives either. Tampa Bay, whose offense ranks 30th today, still ran for 241 yards here.

Where it goes depends on the schedule, and the schedule is kind. The next stretch features Philadelphia without Jalen Hurts, Arizona, Indianapolis and Tennessee, and the division leader sits at 3-2-1. If the turnovers settle back toward the early-season level, this offense can win shootouts against mediocre teams. The defense is unlikely to improve meaningfully, though. It is a two-year pattern, not an early-season wobble, so the realistic ceiling is a scrappy NFC East race, not a contender.

strengths.title: Prescott plays from clean pockets
strengths.body: Dallas allows sacks at the second-lowest rate in the league, even with a time to throw that ranks only 23rd, so this isn't a quick-game illusion. The line is holding up and Prescott is avoiding negative plays. Protection like this tends to be stable, and it keeps the offense's floor high even in bad weeks.

strengths.title: A genuinely efficient offense
strengths.body: Sixth in EPA per play with a pass-leaning approach (2.4 points over expected), the offense has scored 30-plus three times. It ranked 5th in EPA last year too, so this is a repeatable unit, not a hot start. The concentrated target tree through Lamb and Pickens gives it a reliable identity.

strengths.title: Run game better than its YPC
strengths.body: The 3.33 yards per carry looks ugly, but run success ranks 6th and run EPA 9th. Williams is stuffed often, but when he isn't, he keeps the chains moving. The run game is a complement that prevents obvious passing downs, not a weakness to fix.

concerns.title: Pass defense is the league's worst
concerns.body: Dallas allows 0.327 EPA per dropback, 32nd, and it carries over from a defense that ranked 32nd last season, so this is structural. The damage comes underneath: 31st on short passes and 31st in explosive pass rate, which means yards after the catch and missed tackles turning short throws into chunk plays. With a 22nd-ranked pressure rate, there is no pass rush to cover for it.

concerns.title: Can't get off the field
concerns.body: Opponents convert 54.7% of third downs, worst in the league. That keeps Dallas's good offense on the sideline and drags its time of possession to 30th. Combined with 3 takeaways (30th), the defense almost never ends drives early. Some of the takeaway drought should regress, but the third-down problem follows directly from the coverage issues.

concerns.title: Recent turnover spike
concerns.body: After four clean-ish weeks, the offense gave it away three times against Tampa Bay and twice at Green Bay, and pass EPA went negative in both. The turnover differential is now -4, which a team with no defensive margin can't absorb. Turnover-prone stretches usually cool off, but last year's -0.6 per game (30th) makes this a pattern worth watching rather than pure noise.

trend.note: The offense carried the first four games, including 37, 31 and 34-point outputs. Then the last two produced 16 and 13 points with five turnovers and negative passing EPA, while the defense never got better at any point.

nextGame.headline: A depleted, Hurts-less Eagles team is the get-right spot Dallas needs
nextGame.body:
Dallas goes to Philadelphia as a 4.5-point favorite (moneyline -225, total 44.5), and the matchup mostly explains why. The Eagles' offense ranks 28th in EPA and 31st in success rate, with a line that has the worst stuff rate in the league and a 7% sack rate. Their defense can't pressure the quarterback (27th in pressure rate, 32nd in QB hit rate), misses tackles at the second-worst rate, and ranks 30th against the run by EPA. That fits neatly with Dallas's clean-pocket, keep-it-on-schedule offense. Philadelphia's one clear edge is special teams, at 2.71 EPA a game (6th) to Dallas's 0.1.

Availability tilts heavily toward Dallas. Jalen Hurts is on IR, expected to miss the rest of the season with blood clots in his lungs, so Tanner McKee makes his second start. He does so without right tackle Lane Johnson, guard Landon Dickerson or Saquon Barkley, and with linebacker Jalyx Hunt and corner Michael Carter II out and Nolan Smith Jr. questionable after a concussion. Dallas is missing corner Cobie Durant and likely linebacker Dee Winters, and KaVontae Turpin is expected to sit. DeMarvion Overshown is listed out but reported on track to return, which would help a linebacker group that is thin otherwise.

waysToWin.title: Lamb feasts on the WR1 matchup
waysToWin.body: Philadelphia has given opposing top receivers 3.0 PPR points a game over their average and 0.54 EPA per target (28th). Lamb is Dallas's clear WR1 on target share, and with the Eagles struggling to pressure, Prescott should have time to find him repeatedly. This is the most direct path to the 25-plus points Dallas usually scores when it's healthy.

waysToWin.title: Clean pocket against no pass rush
waysToWin.body: Dallas's 2nd-ranked sack rate meets a defense that ranks 32nd in QB hit rate and 31st in sack rate. If Prescott is rarely touched, the passing game should look like Weeks 2-4 rather than the last two games. The Eagles also miss tackles at a 12.1% clip, so short completions can become chunk gains.

waysToWin.title: Even this defense can stop McKee
waysToWin.body: Philadelphia's offense was already 28th in EPA with Hurts and now loses him, Johnson, Dickerson and Barkley. A line with the league's worst stuff rate gives Dallas's mediocre front a chance to set up third-and-long. A couple of stops early forces a backup quarterback to chase the game, the one script where this Dallas defense can win.

waysToLose.title: Turnovers hand over short fields
waysToLose.body: The Eagles can't move the ball consistently on their own, so their best path is Dallas giving it to them. Another three-turnover day like Week 5 would let McKee play on short fields against a defense that already allows two-thirds of red-zone trips to become touchdowns. Philadelphia is also 13th in one-score win rate and comfortable in grinders.

waysToLose.title: Third downs keep McKee alive
waysToLose.body: Dallas allows 54.7% on third down, worst in football, and its pass defense is softest on exactly the short throws a backup quarterback lives on. If McKee can dink his way to conversions, Philadelphia drains the clock, keeps Prescott on the bench and turns this into a low-possession coin flip.

waysToLose.title: Special teams swing a close game
waysToLose.body: Philadelphia's special teams add 2.71 EPA a game (6th), against Dallas's neutral unit, and Turpin is expected to miss the game. In a game the Book totals at 44.5, a long return or a hidden-yardage edge could be the difference, especially given Dallas's 25% record in one-score games.

nextGame.watch: Prescott's ball security on early downs. If Dallas avoids giving McKee short fields, the talent gap should show by the third quarter.

restOfSeason.body:
The offense is real and should keep scoring in the mid-20s. Elite pass protection, a concentrated target tree and an efficient run game have now held up across two seasons. The recent turnover burst should cool somewhat, and the 25% record in close games and the -1.39 wins over expected point to some positive regression in the record. The defense won't fix itself. It ranked last against the pass a year ago and ranks last again, so expect most games to be shootouts, with Dallas winning the ones where Prescott protects the ball.

The schedule cooperates. Seven of the remaining opponents have losing records, and Tennessee, Arizona and Indianapolis all rank in the bottom third on defense. San Francisco, Seattle's defense and Jacksonville's offense are the clear tough spots. In a division led by a 3-2-1 team, an 8-9 or 9-8 finish is a plausible path to a playoff race. A clean break above that would require the defense to suddenly start forcing turnovers.

confidence.note: Six games is a small sample, but the profile mirrors 2025 almost exactly; turnover luck adds variance.
